questions.q: Game A, played alone, is a losing game over time. Game B, played alone, is also a losing game over time. Yet by switching back and forth between A and B according to a certain rule, the combined strategy becomes a winning game overall. What is this result called?

An urn contains 90 balls: 30 are red, and the other 60 are black or yellow in some unknown split. Bet A pays $100 if you draw red; Bet B pays $100 if you draw black — most people strictly prefer Bet A. Now Bet C pays $100 if you draw red or yellow; Bet D pays $100 if you draw black or yellow — most people strictly prefer Bet D. For ANY assumed number of yellow balls, preferring A over B together with D over C is logically inconsistent. What does this classic result (the Ellsberg paradox) demonstrate?
choices: People prefer known probabilities (risk) over unknown ones (ambiguity), even though it produces logically inconsistent preferences
Red is genuinely the better colour to bet on in every case
People are simply bad at arithmetic with fractions
The two pairs of bets are not actually inconsistent once risk aversion is included

questions.q: A forensic expert testifies that a DNA sample matches the defendant, and 'the probability of a random person matching by chance is 1 in 1,000,000' — the expert then concludes 'so there is only a 1 in 1,000,000 chance the defendant is innocent.' What is the flaw in this reasoning?
choices: The 1-in-1,000,000 figure must be wrong because DNA matches are always unique
It conflates the probability of the evidence given innocence with the probability of innocence given the evidence — the latter also depends on how many other people could have been tested
There is no flaw; a 1-in-a-million match is conclusive proof of guilt
DNA evidence is never reliable enough to use in court

Behind one of two doors is freedom, behind the other is death. One guard always tells the truth, the other always lies, but you don't know which is which. You may ask exactly one question, to one guard, to guarantee finding the door to freedom. What do you ask?
